scope: The 47 requested cryptographic, protocol and traffic/privacy validation categories. Each claim is limited to its mapped executable checks or explicit analysis boundary; category presence and a passing test runner do not establish certification, whole-implementation proofs or measured privacy.

items.name: Known Answer Testing (KAT)
items.claim: Shipping X25519 and AEAD interfaces reproduce published RFC/NIST byte answers; ML-DSA key generation, signing and verification are checked against the pinned ACVP fixtures.
limitations: Finite vector conformance does not establish cryptographic strength, constant-time execution or complete algorithm-validation coverage.

items.name: Cryptographic Algorithm Validation
items.claim: Published known answers, independent-backend comparisons and malformed-input tests provide reproducible algorithm-conformance prerequisites; they do not confer a CAVP validation.
limitations: No CAVP certificate is asserted for this application, these self-tests or its arbitrary compiled operational environments.
external_requirements: Formal CAVP validation requires an accredited laboratory and NIST validation of the exact implementation and operational environment: https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program

items.name: Cryptographic Module Validation
items.claim: The repository identifies shipping crypto dependencies and checks module interfaces, secret handling and algorithm prerequisites; it does not claim a validated FIPS cryptographic module boundary.
limitations: A validated dependency or successful algorithm test does not make the complete proxy a CMVP-validated module; module boundary, build mode, platform and security policy remain material.
external_requirements: Formal CMVP validation requires a defined module/security policy and accredited laboratory assessment of the exact build and platform: https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program

items.name: Encryption Correctness Testing
items.claim: Both production record ciphers match published answers and an independent backend in both directions, across nonce carry, rekey and serial/parallel batches.
limitations: The selected finite messages and counters are checked; correctness of every native instruction and arbitrary execution is not proved.

items.name: Authenticated Encryption Verification
items.claim: Published AEAD messages reject each changed ciphertext/tag bit, truncated input and changed key/nonce/AAD; record-level direction reflection, replay and failed-batch publication also fail.
limitations: These are concrete acceptance/output checks, not a computational AEAD security proof or a complete memory-residency analysis.

items.name: Message Authentication Code Verification
items.claim: HMAC-SHA256 reproduces RFC 4231 short/long-key vectors; independent auth-carrier and exporter oracles check context binding and altered messages/credentials.
limitations: Validating finite tags and binders is not a proof of all MAC callsites or all secret-dependent timing behavior.

items.name: Digital Signature Verification Testing
items.claim: ML-DSA verification agrees with ACVP and an independent implementation; production identity checks reject a wrong pin or changed transcript, epoch and PQ exchange.
limitations: The symbolic model assumes ideal signatures; ACVP/differential cases do not certify side-channel resistance or all possible malformed signatures.

items.name: Cryptographic Key Generation Testing
items.claim: X25519 published keys and ML-DSA ACVP key generation match their answers; OS-backed X25519, ML-KEM and ML-DSA smoke tests check consistency and distinct sampled public keys.
limitations: Distinct sampled keys and valid signatures/decapsulation do not measure entropy or prove resistance to OS RNG compromise.

items.name: Key Derivation Function Testing (KDF)
items.claim: HKDF-Extract matches RFC 5869; independent frozen answers check protocol-specific HKDF/HMAC labels and generated oracles check initial, hybrid, epoch, direction and substream derivation.
limitations: Protocol-specific info/labels have independently frozen answers; they are not presented as the RFC's published arbitrary-info OKM vectors or as a computational KDF proof.

items.name: Key Management Testing
items.claim: Live secret containers expose redacted Debug output and zeroization/drop contracts; record keys separate contexts and rekey does not clear sticky failure poison.
limitations: Tests inspect owned live buffers and declared drop contracts, not freed storage. Compiler copies, registers, allocator remnants, swap, crash dumps and physical secure erasure remain outside this claim.
Equality compile-fail doctests are additional API controls and must run with cargo test --locked --doc; a normal library run does not execute them.
external_requirements: Host memory/secret-residency assessment is required for deployment-specific erasure guarantees.

items.name: Random Number Generator Testing
items.claim: Bounded OS RNG smoke tests generate consistent X25519/ML-KEM/ML-DSA material and live authentication nonces without collisions in the selected samples.
limitations: Eight X25519, four ML-KEM, three ML-DSA key pairs and 64 nonces are smoke samples. They are not entropy estimation, a DRBG validation, a prediction-resistance test or evidence that the host RNG is uncompromised.
external_requirements: Entropy-source/DRBG assurances require the actual OS/hardware source and its applicable validation evidence.

items.name: Initialization Vector / Nonce Reuse Testing
items.claim: Serial/parallel record reservations and QUIC protected packet numbers do not reuse an issued nonce, wrap budgets or roll back failure consumption; a new key establishes a new epoch.
limitations: Models and generated histories have documented bounds. Reusing identical keys/state outside these session constructors or after external process-state rollback is not ruled out by finite execution tests.

items.name: Cryptographic Parameter Validation
items.claim: Degenerate X25519, empty PSKs, malformed KEM lengths, unsupported suite tags and changed AEAD parameters fail before accepted session material or plaintext is returned.
limitations: ML-KEM implicit rejection intentionally returns a pseudorandom secret for a well-sized invalid ciphertext; the rejection is tested at derived-key/record authentication rather than assuming every corruption is a parse error.

items.name: Cryptographic Error Handling Testing
items.claim: Malformed/tampered crypto inputs do not publish plaintext or usable session state; implicit KEM rejection yields incompatible record keys and failed parallel records permanently poison further publication.
limitations: The controlled failure paths do not cover arbitrary hardware faults, every panic or all allocation/lifetime behavior.

items.name: Side-channel Analysis
items.claim: The existing feature-gated timing experiment compares selected attacker-reachable inbound rejection shapes with calibrated controls; secret-container checks separately limit direct Debug/API disclosure.
limitations: The timing selector requires --features dudect and a serial statistical run; a featureless library execution is not evidence that it ran.
Selected wall-clock observations do not measure cache, branch predictor, power/EM, speculative-execution or every primitive's secret-dependent behavior.
external_requirements: Deployment-specific hardware/native-assembly side-channel analysis and controlled measurements remain required for broader resistance claims.

items.name: Timing Attack Testing
items.claim: A feature-enabled serial dudect-style experiment tests observed rejection latency against calibrated controls for the selected malformed/authentication failure classes.
limitations: Sample counts, thresholds, CPU, build profile and noise bounds must accompany results. Passing this detector does not establish timing equality or exclude smaller/stronger timing attacks.
external_requirements: Independent timing experiments on supported release CPUs and realistic remote paths are needed for deployment conclusions.

items.name: Constant-time Implementation Verification
items.claim: Selected rejection paths have operation-count/control checks and a wall-clock regression experiment; no whole-module constant-time theorem is claimed.
limitations: Constant-time primitives and subtle comparisons do not prove the surrounding control flow constant-time. Native crypto assembly, compiler transformations and ML-DSA signing rejection loops require separate assessment.
external_requirements: A stronger constant-time claim requires explicit source/assembly information-flow analysis and target-specific validation beyond sampled timing.

items.name: Replay Attack Testing
items.claim: Freshness, committed/pending carrier replay, record nonce reuse and QUIC packet replay are rejected at their actual gates, including bounded persistence/restart cases.
limitations: QUIC marker/ticket guard persistence is asynchronous; a crash before persistence can reopen the newest decision across restart. Tests do not remove that documented durability window.

items.name: Man-in-the-Middle Attack Testing (MITM)
items.claim: Wrong origin trust/name, static-DH pin, PSK, ML-DSA pin and transcript/PQ message binding fail before a target is used; symbolic checks also allow an active network attacker.
limitations: The TCP origin chain and pinned ParallaX identity are distinct trust boundaries. The QUIC cover certificate is intentionally not an independent web-PKI authentication boundary; its session binding is checked through the TCP exporter and identity.

items.name: Downgrade Attack Testing
items.claim: TLS requires its supported TLS 1.3 selection, authenticated cipher-suite bytes remain identity-bound, and authentic QUIC packets carrying a different version cannot commit state.
limitations: The symbolic suite-unbound control validates binding sensitivity; it is not an executable downgrade against the full encrypted protocol. Deliberate UDP decline to authenticated TCP remains supported behavior.

items.name: Forward Secrecy Verification
items.claim: The mapped two-phase symbolic rekey model checks that completed phase-zero application secrets stay secret after phase-one server signing-key disclosure, with PSK and epoch-zero root exposed from the start.
limitations: Unfinished phase-zero roles are discarded at the global transition. Concurrent corruption, sessions continuing across disclosure, secure erasure and a computational hybrid/full-implementation theorem are not established.
The negative controls must detect actual traffic-key disclosure and signing-key disclosure before authentication, while retaining reachable acceptance and disclosure.

items.name: Mutual Authentication Verification
items.claim: Production admission authenticates possession of the shared PSK while the client authenticates a pinned server identity; tests cover these two distinct gates.
limitations: A shared PSK authenticates group membership, not a unique client identity. The symbolic identity model deliberately exposes that PSK and does not claim client-to-server authentication or a mutual-authentication theorem.
external_requirements: Individual-client mutual authentication would require a separately specified credential/protocol design and its own validation.

items.name: Key Confirmation Testing
items.claim: Actual TLS Finished checks, matching exporter results, authenticated UDP probes and exact relay DONE records validate the implemented peer-key confirmation gates.
limitations: Derived-key correspondence in the symbolic rekey slice is not by itself a proof of mutual explicit key confirmation for every protocol stage.

items.name: Authentication and Key Exchange (AKE) Security Analysis
items.claim: The mapped ProVerif slice checks injective pinned-server correspondence, client-direction derived-key agreement and application secrecy against an active symbolic network attacker, with accepting executions required.
limitations: Perfect-cryptography constructors, fresh ephemeral secrets and trusted pins are assumptions. Initial carrier/TLS agreement, concrete primitive security, all state-machine stages and arbitrary corruption are not proved by this slice.

items.name: Key Compromise Impersonation (KCI) Analysis
items.claim: The client-side pinned-server correspondence is checked even when the shared PSK and epoch-zero root are public; the early-signing-disclosure control must instead expose impersonation and secrecy attacks.
limitations: This is a narrow client-side check after shared-PSK compromise, not a general KCI theorem. The server-side individual-client authentication direction is not modeled; shared credentials cannot identify an individual client.
external_requirements: A full two-direction KCI analysis requires an explicit individual-client credential model and corruption policy.

items.name: Session Key Independence Verification
items.claim: Independent derivation answers and fresh production PQ sessions agree within a session while rejecting cross-session, direction, epoch and substream record use.
limitations: Concrete distinctness/authentication checks are not a computational key-independence theorem or a proof of security after arbitrary session-state disclosure.

items.name: Protocol State Machine Testing
items.claim: Finite protocol models and production transition tests check admission/replay, key epochs, identity, reassembly, MUX ownership/half-close, QUIC handshake/keys/close and UDP retention ordering.
limitations: Finite domains and source-order correspondence are documented; these models are not a refinement proof of all Rust, OS and scheduler executions.

items.name: Protocol Version Negotiation Testing
items.claim: TLS version/session-ID/extension selections are validated; authenticated packets with unsupported QUIC versions do not consume packet numbers or other receive state, and supported v1 traffic recovers.
limitations: The implementation supports its specified QUIC v1 behavior; these rejection checks do not claim multi-version interoperability or a complete version-negotiation extension.

items.name: Message Integrity Verification
items.claim: Ciphertext/tag/AAD changes, reflected directions, altered identity-bound transcript fields, malformed lengths and incomplete stream frames cannot become accepted plaintext or a successful handshake/close.
limitations: Integrity checks cover the specified authenticated fields; transport metadata, lengths and timing are not made confidential by authenticating the payload.

items.name: Certificate Chain Validation Testing
items.claim: The binary TCP camouflage client checks trust/name, validity period, usage, signature and intermediate-chain completeness against local CA fixtures, with a valid intermediate-chain positive control.
limitations: QUIC intentionally accepts its cover certificate and relies on session exporter/PQ identity binding; these web-PKI chain claims concern the TCP origin verifier. Certificate revocation is a separate unsupported policy boundary.

items.name: Certificate Revocation Checking
items.claim: The current TCP web-PKI verification call supplies no CRL/OCSP revocation information; this inventory records that absence rather than treating ordinary chain validation as revocation checking.
limitations: CRL/OCSP revocation enforcement and freshness/fail-open policy are not implemented. QUIC's cover-certificate acceptance also supplies no independent revocation guarantee.
external_requirements: Revocation support needs an explicit trust/revocation source, freshness and failure policy, privacy/network-access design and revoked/stale/unavailable-source tests before an enforcement claim.

items.name: Early Data / 0-RTT Replay Analysis
items.claim: Real resumption accepts fresh early data; used tickets fall back to 1-RTT, invalid PSK/binder offers cannot consume the single-use guard, and the documented persistence/restart path is exercised.
limitations: Asynchronous marker/ticket persistence has a documented crash-before-write window. TLS 0-RTT does not inherit a blanket replay-freedom or forward-secrecy guarantee from ordinary 1-RTT tests.

items.name: Packet Reordering Testing
items.claim: Reordered authenticated packet/key phases and reverse-order stream fragments preserve reassembly, replay rejection and bounded receive-state accounting.
limitations: Controlled traces and generated histories do not enumerate every Internet loss/reordering schedule, path MTU or platform socket behavior.

items.name: Duplicate Packet Handling Testing
items.claim: Receive-range eviction does not reopen old packet numbers, and duplicate out-of-order stream fragments cannot deliver duplicate application bytes or grow state without the tested bounds.
limitations: These bounded duplicate/replay traces are distinct from a full packet-loss/reordering performance evaluation.

items.name: Connection Migration Security Testing
items.claim: The current endpoint retains four-tuple ownership: authenticated packets from a different source tuple cannot take over an existing connection, while its original tuple remains usable.
limitations: Connection migration, NAT rebinding and PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE path validation are not supported. Tuple-isolation checks do not establish secure migration support.
external_requirements: Enabling migration requires a separately specified path-validation/address-ownership design and migration/rebinding attack tests.

items.name: Anti-Amplification Verification
items.claim: A real resumed 0-RTT application flight does not validate the peer address or lift the server's three-times received-byte transmit bound; a later valid handshake permits remaining output.
limitations: The test checks the QUIC connection's encoded-byte accounting and address-validation transition; it does not measure whole-host reflection bandwidth, arbitrary IP spoofing or infrastructure rate limits.

items.name: Denial-of-Service Resistance Testing
items.claim: Known malformed/resource-pressure paths enforce replay/source admission, bounded identity/fragment/frame allocation, per-connection/endpoint flow budgets and sibling-stream isolation.
limitations: Finite allocation/admission/scheduling controls are not an availability guarantee against volumetric traffic, authenticated abusive peers, host resource exhaustion or every network schedule.
external_requirements: Deployment capacity and volumetric resistance require controlled load measurements on the actual host/network budget.

items.name: Traffic Analysis
items.claim: The traffic analyzer extracts bounded observable sizes, directions and timing from complete hash-checked captures and evaluates independent held-out groups with uncertainty estimates.
limitations: Analyzer/mechanical tests are not measured traffic privacy. No newly captured representative corpus or deployed-censor result is supplied by passing those tests.
external_requirements: Evaluate fresh independent browser/proxy captures with matched workloads, sites, days, networks and vantage points; retain hashes, controls, holdouts and confidence intervals.

items.name: Traffic Fingerprinting
items.claim: Known ACK/record-size/cadence perturbations exercise detector sensitivity, while corpus analysis fits features/models on training captures and calibrates/test-evaluates separate groups.
limitations: Fixture parity or a chance score from selected models cannot exclude stronger/adaptive classifiers or establish traffic indistinguishability.
external_requirements: A fingerprinting conclusion needs real independent holdout traffic and explicitly reported detector family, false-positive rate and deployment population.

items.name: Website Fingerprinting
items.claim: The website experiment classifies whole held-out sessions with train-only standardization/centroids and reports accuracy, chance and confusion rather than a privacy PASS.
limitations: Synthetic known-site controls validate the machinery only. The repository does not provide a new representative corpus of complete rendered website sessions or establish website-fingerprinting resistance.
external_requirements: Provide independent complete sessions from at least two sites with the tool's per-site group minimum, strict train/test separation and truthful measurement provenance; browser fetch-only workloads cannot stand in for full rendered-site visits.

items.name: Correlation Attack Analysis
items.claim: The two-vantage correlation experiment ranks independent traces using direction/byte time bins and bounded-lag Pearson correlation, preserving ties and checking known/shuffled pairing controls.
limitations: Machinery controls are not a real two-vantage attack measurement. A low score for this correlator does not imply anonymity or resistance to an observer of both endpoints.
external_requirements: Provide separately captured ingress/egress vantage traces, independent sessions, truthful pairing labels, clock/provenance information and held-out evaluation; one trace copied to both sides is not evidence.

items.name: Metadata Leakage Analysis
items.claim: Production encrypted CONNECT records conceal the selected cleartext destination/payload markers while server-side decoding recovers their exact fields; shaping checks place the selected small requests in configured browser record bands.
limitations: Needle absence in controlled ciphertext is not a noninterference theorem. Proxy/origin IPs, cover SNI, record sizes, timing, traffic volume and host/operator logs remain separate visible metadata.
external_requirements: Broader metadata conclusions require real packet/log capture and a declared observer model.

items.name: DNS Leak Testing
items.claim: An unresolved SOCKS DOMAIN can complete through the actual proxy without successful client-side target resolution; independent encrypted-CONNECT decoding confirms exact domain preservation.
limitations: The invalid-domain fixture proves no successful target lookup is required; by itself it cannot detect an unnecessary DNS query whose failure is ignored.
SOCKS only covers applications using remote-domain requests. The app may resolve before SOCKS, proxy server_addr resolution is separate, and no TUN/system DNS interception is provided.
external_requirements: A zero-target-DNS-query conclusion requires an isolated observer/DNS sink or packet capture covering the actual client process and configured app flow; whole-system DNS leak prevention requires separately specified controls.

items.name: IP Leak Testing
items.claim: When the configured proxy is unavailable, an explicit SOCKS flow cannot silently fall back to a direct target connection, checked by an owned target listener's accept count.
limitations: This is a failed-SOCKS-flow direct-connect test. It is not a system kill switch, TUN routing policy, WebRTC/UDP/QUIC browser leak test or proof that unrelated applications never expose the host IP.
external_requirements: Whole-device IP leak prevention needs explicit OS/application routing and failure-policy controls plus separate IPv4/IPv6/DNS/UDP/WebRTC capture tests.

items.name: Protocol Identification Testing
items.claim: TLS/H2/H3 wire-shape checks and captured baseline/distinguisher machinery expose known protocol-identification features, with independent held-out corpus evaluation available for measured conclusions.
limitations: Matching selected templates/fixtures and rejecting malformed inputs do not establish that the complete deployed protocol is unidentified by population or adaptive detectors.
external_requirements: Measure protocol identification on fresh matched normal/proxy traffic with independent negative controls and held-out browser/version/network populations.

items.name: Active Probing Resistance Testing
items.claim: Known unauthenticated, wrong-credential and malformed admissions preserve origin splice behavior without target dial, and authenticated recovery remains usable; timing is a separate statistical check.
limitations: The probe shapes and owned local origins are finite. Their behavior does not establish indistinguishability from every live origin, network fault, timing attack or deployed censor.
external_requirements: Operational active-probe resistance needs authorized real-path measurements with matched origin/error/timing controls.

items.name: Traffic Classification Evaluation
items.claim: Classifier tooling separates whole capture groups across train/calibration/test, excludes identifier metadata as features, calibrates only on normal calibration traffic and reports AUC/TPR/FPR with uncertainty.
limitations: Synthetic controls and analysis integrity tests validate mechanics; they cannot supply missing real captures or turn evaluated/insufficient_evidence into a security PASS. Optional backend absence and insufficient group/FPR support remain explicit.
external_requirements: Retain real independent capture artifacts, manifest hashes, implementation/browser versions, dataset/holdout provenance, model versions, seed, thresholds and confidence intervals for any traffic-classification claim.
